review: Original lesson objectives and sources retained. Correct absolute claims to the models actually taught; offer model-arm access at the earlier tasks as well as the workshop. Shorten actual new Lundy and practice instructions.

sources.supports: Fruit/vegetables and starchy foods each just over a third; balance over a day or week.
Not all food chains start with plants; examples remain green-plant classroom chains.

changes.from: Use the final four minutes for one pupil-chosen card: point to the structural evidence, compare it with size/fur/legs, then keep or correct the answer. Pass and private adult responses are welcome.
changes.to: Use the last four minutes to choose one card. Point to a body clue. Does size, fur or the number of legs prove it has a backbone? Keep or change your answer. You may pass or tell the adult in private.

changes.from: Explain how you can tell an invertebrate without cutting it open.
changes.to: How could you check if an animal has a backbone without cutting it open?

changes.from: Look for a hard case or shell outside, or a soft body with no line of bones down the back.
changes.to: Use a clear body diagram or a trusted body fact. A soft outside alone is not proof. We do not cut or handle an animal.

changes.from: Split pins and elastic bands are fiddly. Ask for the pre-assembled kit if that is the bit that gets in the way — the science is the labels, not the fixing.
changes.to: Ask for a ready-made card arm if the joins are hard to make. You can tell an adult how to move it. We want to see the science in your labels.

changes.from: Use the final four minutes to compare two animals and two food choices from the lesson. Explain why the same quantity is not enough if the type is unsuitable. Use model cards, never feed an animal.
changes.to: Use the last four minutes to compare two animals and two food cards. Would the same food suit both? Say why the type of food matters as well as how much there is. Use only cards. Never feed an animal.

changes.from: One food type is unlikely to provide the whole range of nutrients needed. Many foods contribute to more than one job.
changes.to: One type of food may not give all the nutrients we need. One food can help with more than one body job.

changes.from: Food is a personal subject. You never have to talk about what you eat at home — the cards do the talking today.
changes.to: You do not have to say what you eat at home. Use the food cards today.

changes.from: Why every chain has to start with a plant
changes.to: Why these chains start with a plant

changes.from: Only a plant can make its own food.
changes.to: The plant makes its own food in this chain.

changes.from: Every food chain starts with a plant because plants are the only ones that can make their own food. Animals are consumers, so they have to eat.
changes.to: These chains start with a green plant. It makes food using light. The animals are consumers. They get food by eating.

changes.from: Explain why every food chain has to start with a plant.
changes.to: Explain why the two chains in this lesson start with a plant.

changes.from: Only plants can make their own food, so the energy has to enter the chain there.
changes.to: The green plant makes food using light. The animals in our chain get food by eating.
